brief: Something to keep my sewing supplies tidy.

requirements.requirement: Keep sewing supplies tidy (separate places for different items)
requirements.evidence: The 3-compartment bin at 0,0, the 2-compartment bin at 1,0 and the open bin at 0,1 give 6 separate storage spaces.

requirements.requirement: Holds together as one sturdy unit
requirements.evidence: lockJoints added 3 joint bolts between the bases, and capOpenFaces closed the 12 open faces with end caps.
The catalog has no sewing props, so a marker (prop:1), a pen (prop:2) and a pencil cup (prop:3) stand in for the supplies. All three can be seen.

finish.summary: I built a small three-cell organiser for sewing supplies. Three hex bases sit in a tight triangle (cells 0,0 / 1,0 / 0,1), each with a full-depth bin. The bin at 0,0 has 3 compartments for small things like pins, needles and bobbins. The bin at 1,0 has 2 compartments for spools of thread, tape or scissors. The bin at 0,1 is open with no dividers, for bigger items like fabric scraps or a pin cushion. All open faces have solid end caps and the joints are bolted so the bases can't slide apart. The total is 18 parts, about 1600 g of filament and about 37 hours of printing. The prop catalog has no sewing items (no thread, scissors or pins), so I dressed it with a stand-in marker, a pen and a pencil cup to show how it gets used. The configurator check passed and the mesh check came back clear.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
